title: Rigor and Transparency Index, a new metric of quality for assessing biological and medical science methods
abstract: Abstract The reproducibility crisis in science is a multifaceted problem involving practices and incentives, both in the laboratory and in publication. Fortunately, some of the root causes are known and can be addressed by scientists and authors alike. After careful consideration of the available literature, the National Institutes of Health identified several key problems with the way that scientists conduct and report their research and introduced guidelines to improve the rigor and reproducibility of pre-clinical studies. Many journals have implemented policies addressing these same criteria. We currently have, however, no comprehensive data on how these guidelines are impacting the reporting of research. Using SciScore, an automated tool developed to review the methods sections of manuscripts for the presence of criteria associated with the NIH and other reporting guidelines, e.g., ARRIVE, RRIDs, we have analyzed ~1.6 million PubMed Central papers to determine the degree to which articles were addressing these criteria. The tool scores each paper on a ten point scale identifying sentences that are associated with compliance with criteria associated with increased rigor (5 pts) and those associated with key resource identification and authentication (5 pts). From these data, we have built the Rigor and Transparency Index, which is the average score for analyzed papers in a particular journal. Our analyses show that the average score over all journals has increased since 1997, but remains below five, indicating that less than half of the rigor and reproducibility criteria are routinely addressed by authors. To analyze the data further, we examined the prevalence of individual criteria across the literature, e.g., the reporting of a subject’s sex (21-37% of studies between 1997 and 2019), the inclusion of sample size calculations (2-10%), whether the study addressed blinding (3-9%), or the identifiability of key biological resources such as antibodies (11-43%), transgenic organisms (14-22%), and cell lines (33-39%). The greatest increase in prevalence for rigor criteria was seen in the use of randomization of subjects (10-30%), while software tool identifiability improved the most among key resource types (42-87%). We further analyzed individual journals over time that had implemented specific author guidelines covering rigor criteria, and found that in some journals, they had a big impact, whereas in others they did not. We speculate that unless they are enforced, author guidelines alone do little to improve the number of criteria addressed by authors. Our Rigor and Transparency Index did not correlate with the impact factors of journals.

Short impact summary

Rigor and Transparency Index, a new metric of quality for assessing biological and medical science methods (2020) in bioRxiv (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory). 16 citations.

Full narrative

Rigor and Transparency Index, a new metric of quality for assessing biological and medical science methods (2020) in bioRxiv (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory) is authored by Joseph Menke, Martijn Roelandse and İbrahim Burak Özyurt. Topics: Transparency (behavior), Rigour, Index (typography), Medical journal and Metric (unit).

16 citations (OpenAlex). Citations peaked in 2021 with 7 citing works. Citing venues include Nature, bioRxiv (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory) and Journal of Biomedical Informatics.

narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

This preprint has shown clear early scholarly uptake, with 16 citations and downstream reuse across articles, preprints, book chapters, and a biomedical article mention. Its influence is concentrated in research on transparency, reproducibility, and methods for assessing scientific reporting, and it has also drawn visible community discussion on Hypothesis.

Full narrative

Rigor and Transparency Index, a new metric of quality for assessing biological and medical science methods addresses a central problem in biomedical research: how to make rigor and transparency more measurable and actionable. The record shows that the article quickly moved beyond its preprint stage into a published version, and that it began circulating in conversations about reproducibility soon after release.

The strongest sign of impact is scholarly reuse. The article has been cited 16 times in OpenAlex, with citations appearing in 2020 and 2021 and continuing into later years. The citing literature is broad enough to suggest method-level relevance rather than a narrow, one-off use: it includes work in biomedical informatics, reproducibility research, natural language processing, and discussions of reporting transparency. It is also cited in a Nature paper and in other prominent research venues, indicating that the metric concept reached audiences working on research quality and scholarly communication.

Beyond formal citations, the work shows evidence of active methodological uptake. It has been reused in related articles and preprints that build on transparency, risk-of-bias assessment, preregistration, and reporting frameworks. This pattern suggests that the paper helped shape a developing toolkit for evaluating and improving research practices, especially in life sciences and medical research settings.

Public discussion is present but modest in scale. The record shows 8 online mentions, concentrated on Hypothesis, where readers commented directly on the preprint and its revisions. That discussion, together with the article’s later citation trail, suggests a paper that was noticed early by an engaged methods community and then carried forward into subsequent work on reproducibility and reporting standards.

Overall, the evidence points to a methodologically influential paper with steady scholarly use, visible community engagement, and documented downstream reuse. The impact record is strongest in technical and reproducibility-focused circles, where the article appears to have contributed to broader efforts to measure and improve rigor in biological and medical science methods.
